newsitem.title: FRANCE: Monory nominates Boissonat, Achard to BoF council.
newsitem.headline: Monory nominates Boissonat, Achard to BoF council.

text.p: French Senate head Rene Monory said on Wednesday he wanted to reappoint Bank of France monetary policy council member Jean Boissonnat to the council and was also nominating Pierre Achard, economic counsellor at the French embassy in Bonn.

Monory, National Assembly head Philippe Seguin and Jean Matteoli, head of the Economic and Social Council (CES), are all putting forward two candidates each for two posts coming up in January on the nine-member council, which is responsible for setting French interest rate policy. The terms of office of Boissonnat, a former journalist who has defended governor Jean-Claude Trichet's stance on monetary and currency stability, and banker Bruno de Maulde, come up for renewal on January 6.
Monory told French radio that he did not think President Jacques Chirac had yet decided on the candidates.
"I do not believe he has made his choice," he said.
"We are proposing three lists of two names. What I want is to preserve the orthodoxy of the Bank of France," he said.

"Therefore I am proposing two names. I am proposing Jean Boissonnt and Achard, who is a very serious young man, who is in Germany at the moment. Mr Matteoli is proposing others, M. Seguin is proposing others," he said.

He said in any case he wanted the Bank of France to stick to current policies. "Why would you want to question this policy. If you question this policy, you will not have markets which are as good as they are at the moment," he said.

Under the terms of the law making the Bank of France independent in 1994, Bank of France council members must be named by the French cabinet on the basis of a list submitted by the presidents of the Senate, National Assembly and CES.
The list is submitted for comment to the Bank of France council.
The law making the Bank independent requires the replacements of Boissonat and de Maulde to be named at least eight days before the expiry of their mandate.
Sources familiar with the process said Seguin, Monory and Matteoli had failed to agree on a joint panel of nominees and had therefore decided to submit separate lists.

The sources said the main disagreement was between Monory, an ardent pro-European, and Seguin, who campaigned against the Maastricht treaty in a 1992 referendum and favours a softer franc and faster interest rate cuts.
Financial markets are watching closely because of concern that the government might use the possible replacement of the two to try to soften the Bank's policy on interest rates.

The sources said Seguin had put forward Robert Pelletier, formerly managing director of the association of credit establishments (Afec) and Alain Prate, a treasury offical and an ex-deputy governor of the central bank.
Matteoli put forward Pierre Guillen, former head of the CNPF employers federation and Jean-Rene Bernard, formerly head of regional bank CIC and deputy governor of Credit Foncier.
